Live from NPR News in Washington, D.C., I'm Dale Willman.
Three judges from the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals held an unusual Sunday hearing
in the Department of Justice's lawsuit against California over its voter rolls.
As NPR's Drew Joffe-Bloch reports, the DOJ is trying to demand election
officials set aside the ballots of 20,000 registered voters.
The DOJ says the registered voters in question are likely non-citizens and is arguing that
California election officials must be stopped from processing their ballots.
Lawyers for the state in Los Angeles County have argued that the DOJ's list is unreliable
and doing what the federal government demands would be unlawful and logistically infeasible.
A federal judge set a hearing in the case for this Tuesday.
But before that could happen, the DOJ appealed to the Ninth Circuit,
arguing the lower court wasn't moving fast enough.
In the Sunday hearing, two of the three judges on the panel had hard questions for the DOJ attorney,
both about the department's demands and whether the appeals court can even weigh in at this stage.
Drew Joffe-Bloch, NPR News.
President Trump was in port here on Michigan Today campaigning
for the Republican candidate for U.S. Senator.
We're going to elect, I call him Apple Pie.
He's like perfect, this guy.
He's like central testing.
He's what your state is all about.
He really is.
He's a fantastic man.
He's going to be one of the great United States senators, Mike Rogers.
Rogers is facing Abdul El-Sayed in a tight race that observers say could determine control
of the U.S. Senate for the next two years.
During the same rally, Trump intensified his anti-Muslim rhetoric against El-Sayed,
questioning his loyalty to the U.S. and portraying him as a threat to national security.
In Brazil, left-wing President Lula has come back from behind to win the presidential election
after ranking second in an initial round of voting.
Catherine Osborne reports from Rio de Janeiro.
A downtown Rio Plaza pulsed with surprised relief after President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva
was elected for a fourth non-consecutive term.
He defeated right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former President Chair Bolsonaro.
The possibility of another Bolsonaro presidency sent Lula supporters into the streets to campaign
by the tens of thousands in recent weeks.
Their attempt to swing votes paid off.
Lula's victory runs counter to a right-wing wave sweeping Latin America.
He's promised to continue standing up to President Trump's
aggressive approach toward the region.
For NPR News, I'm Catherine Osborne in Rio de Janeiro.
A second storm has hit the U.K. this weekend,
and it's causing widespread travel disruptions and power outages.
Government officials say Storm Bolo is posing a danger to life from flying debris and crashing
waves.
Gusts above 80 miles an hour have been recorded in Scotland,
and flood warnings are in place in several areas.
You're listening to NPR News.
More than 80 people have been injured,
with at least seven in serious condition after a bus plunged off a road in Spain Sunday.
Officials say the bus plunged down a 65-foot embankment after driving off a narrow road.
Rescue crews are searching for any other victims.
The accident is now under investigation.
Students on both sides of the U.S.-Mexico border are helping to monitor the health of
the Rio Grande as part of an annual environmental education initiative.
Texas Public Radio's Tim Gutierrez reports from Laredo.
Hundreds of Laredo students are cleaning up Sakate Creek,
a tributary of the Rio Grande, as part of Dia del Rio, a month-long celebration of the river.
Nearly 1,800 students in the U.S. and Mexico are also testing water samples for pollution.
Lamar Middle School student Abraham de Leon says protecting the river is critical.
If we don't handle what's wrong with the river, it's just going to go bad,
and that's our only resource of water.
Sharon Munoz of the Rio Grande International Study Center
says students are helping make a difference.
We're giving them the opportunity to be part of the change and to understand
why water monitoring and water testing is so important.
Past testing has found elevated arsenic, ammonia, and bacteria levels.
I'm Tim Gutierrez in Laredo.
Miami remains at number one in the AP College football poll this week.
Ohio State had a bye week but moves up to number two.
Georgia moves up to number three.
Indiana is fourth and Notre Dame dropped to fifth.
Utah now is in sixth, followed by UCLA, BYU, Kentucky, and Alabama in tenth.
I'm Dale Willman, NPR News.
